S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible product-specific safety risk, and promptly provide any updated instructions or corrective action. Suspected incidents must not be omitted while investigation is pending.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a regulator-accepted sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a representative sample and a documented, reproducible protocol. New models must not exceed a 5% failure rate. A model already marketed when this standard takes effect that exceeds 5% may remain available under regulator-approved risk controls and enhanced incident monitoring while the regulator reviews its safety case. Per-model results, including the failure rate and test method, must be made available to customers of that model before purchase; individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems must support secure remote emergency shut-off by the date this standard takes effect, with a safe local shut-off available if communications fail. For already-installed systems, manufacturers must provide compatible remote shut-off capability or an equivalent safe corrective measure within six years of the effective date.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New models placed on the market 36 months or more after adoption of this standard must include built-in fire suppression, validated for the battery chemistry and enclosure. Regulators may approve an equivalent protective design where the manufacturer demonstrates an equal or greater reduction in fire risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model's confirmed thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly report it to regulators and notify affected customers. Following review, regulators must require a recall or other effective corrective remedy proportionate to the verified risk and the demonstrated effectiveness of alternatives.

document.section_notes: S2 keeps a 5% cap for new models but lets existing above-limit models continue indefinitely under regulator review, which mainly protects Northwind's Hearth 10, while per-model results go to customers but not the public. S5 makes the 8-per-100k rate a trigger for reporting, notice and review rather than a mandatory recall, with the regulator choosing an open-ended corrective remedy, which mainly protects Halcyon's Ember 8. S3 gives a 72-month retrofit window (acceptable, not the 36-month safe level), and S4 sets a 36-month built-in suppression lead time.
